entry.title: NPR Music: Tyshawn Sorey’s powerful sounds of silence | Amplify with Lara Downes
entry.summary: Tyshawn Sorey spent spring at Knoxville’s Big Ears Festival exploring the power of space and silence. Inspired by the dark, light-revealing canvases of Rothko’s Houston chapel and Morton Feldman’s 1971 score, Sorey’s new piece Monochromatic Light (Afterlife) strips away conventional structure to let tiny shifts in tone and texture guide the listener through time-bending soundscapes. Bass-baritone Davóne Tines, one of the performers, says the work’s long pauses aren’t gaps but “places of reflection and rest.” In Sorey’s hands, silence becomes a kind of refuge—an invitation to slow down and notice the nearly undetectable moments of light and shade that often slip by in our noisy, fast-paced world. Watch on YouTube

entry.title: The Inheritance Gallery
entry.summary: Timothy's library had grown beyond simple books. He now cataloged audiobooks, ebooks, and rare manuscripts—each with unique attributes. Audiobooks had narrators and durations. Ebooks had file formats and download links. Manuscripts had preservation conditions and historical significance. His first attempt created separate classes with duplicated code: Margaret found him writing the same initialization code for the third time. "You're repeating yourself," she observed. "Come to the Inheritance Gallery—where specialized blueprints inherit from general ones." The Parent-Child Relationship "The Audiobook class inherits from Book," Margaret explained. "It gets all of Book's attributes and methods automatically. We only add what's unique to audiobooks."

entry.title: Researchers find adding this one simple sentence to prompts makes AI models way more creative
entry.summary: One of the coolest things about generative AI models — both large language models (LLMs) and diffusion-based image generators — is that they are "non-deterministic." That is, despite their reputation among some critics as being "fancy autocorrect," generative AI models actually generate their outputs by choosing from a distribution of the most probable next tokens (units of information) to fill out their response. Asking an LLM: "What is the capital of France?" will have it sample its probability distribution for France, capitals, cities, etc. to arrive at the answer "Paris." But that answer could come in the format of "The capital of France is Paris," or simply "Paris" or "Paris, though it was Versailles at one point."
